questions: Are you more of a dog person or a cat person — or neither?
Did you have any pets growing up, or did you want one?
Why do you think some people talk to their pets as if they were people?
Were attitudes to keeping pets different when your grandparents were young?
Do you think more people around you will keep pets in the future, or fewer?
When was the last time you spent a day in the countryside?
Is there a particular rural place you go back to again and again?
What do you enjoy most when you're out of the city — and what do you miss?
Did you spend more time in the countryside as a child than you do now?
Could you ever see yourself living in a village permanently? Why or why not?

part2.title: Describe an animal you find interesting.
bullets: what the animal is and what it looks like
where you first saw it or learned about it
what it does that you find remarkable
how you feel when you watch or think about it
part2.explain: and explain why this animal interests you more than others, and what it has made you think about.
followups: Have you ever seen one in real life, or only on a screen?
Is this an animal most people in your country would recognise?
Would you want to see one in the wild, if you could?

part3.q: Why do people in crowded cities, with so little space, still go to the trouble of keeping pets?
followups: What are pets actually giving those owners?
Has that need grown as families have got smaller?

part3.q: Is it fair on the animal to keep a large dog in a small city flat?
followups: Where would you draw the line?
Should cities regulate this, or is it the owner's business?

part3.q: Some people spend enormous amounts on their pets while people nearby go hungry. Is that a fair criticism of pet owners?
followups: Could you say the same about any luxury spending?
Why do you think pets attract this criticism in particular?

part3.q: Zoos say they exist for conservation and education. Critics say they're prisons with gift shops. Who's closer to the truth?
followups: Does your answer change for a species that would otherwise be extinct?
Is a safari park meaningfully different from a zoo?

part3.q: Most of what people know about wild animals now comes from documentaries. How does that shape what we think nature is actually like?
followups: What do documentaries leave out?
Is a misleadingly beautiful picture of nature better than no picture at all?

part3.q: Can watching animals on a screen ever substitute for seeing them in the wild?
followups: What changes in a person when they see the real thing?
Given the carbon cost of travel, should we be encouraging screen wildlife instead?

part3.q: When a species is disappearing, whose responsibility is it to act — individuals, governments, or someone else?
followups: What can one individual actually do that matters?
What happens when the species lives in a poor country but the demand destroying it comes from rich ones?

part3.q: Conservation money flows to tigers, pandas and elephants — the photogenic species. Is that a sensible way to decide what gets saved?
followups: Why do those species attract the money?
Would the public fund the ugly but ecologically vital ones?

part3.q: Advertisers use animals constantly — lions for banks, owls for insurance. Why do animals sell things so effectively?
followups: Do those images change how we treat the real animals?
Is there anything dishonest about it?

part3.q: Humans have always defined themselves against animals — we speak, they don't; we reason, they don't. Is that line as clear as we like to think?
followups: Has anything you've learned about animals blurred it for you?
If the line is blurry, what follows for how we're allowed to treat them?

fc: Sustains the full Part 2 description — appearance, behaviour, feeling — without collapsing into a list of facts recited from a documentary.
Takes a position quickly on the charged Part 3 questions (zoos, pet spending) and develops it, rather than hedging in circles.
Moves between registers fluidly: affectionate about a childhood pet one minute, analytical about conservation funding the next.
Extends answers unprompted — the documentary question should produce a mechanism and an example, not one sentence and a pause.
Handles the abstract final questions without long silences: "I've never thought of it that way, but I suppose…" and straight into an idea.
lr: Topic vocabulary used precisely: habitat, predator, instinct, domesticated, endangered, ecosystem, camouflage, companionship.
Natural collocations — "in the wild", "on the verge of extinction", "form a bond with", "keep a pet" — not invented pairings.
Describes animal behaviour with verbs that do real work: stalk, hover, burrow, mimic, migrate — instead of 'it does something amazing'.
One vivid comparison ("it moves like smoke") beats a pile of adjectives like 'amazing' and 'incredible'.
Steps up to Part 3 abstraction — welfare, exploitation, stewardship, sentience — without the register wobbling.
gra: Present simple under control for describing behaviour in Part 2 ("it hunts alone", "they mate for life") mixed with past forms for when you first encountered it.
Comparatives and superlatives handled cleanly — the topic invites them constantly ("far more intelligent than people assume").
Conditionals for the ethics questions: "If zoos really existed for conservation, they would…", "If we stopped filming wildlife, people might care even less."
Concessive structures for balance: "Even though I love zoos as a visitor, I struggle to defend them", "Admittedly, documentaries simplify things, but…".
Errors are rare and self-corrected in passing; subject–verb agreement survives long sentences about species and populations.
pron: Clearly intelligible throughout — species names and animal vocabulary must not be swallowed; slow down for the unfamiliar word rather than mumbling it.
Sentence stress carries the wonder in Part 2: "it can find its way home across a THOUSAND kilometres."
Intonation separates affection (the pet story) from argument (the zoo debate) naturally — one lively, one measured.
Connected speech natural ("sort_of", "kind_of_creature", "in_the_wild") rather than word-by-word delivery.
Multi-syllable topic words — endangered, documentary, responsibility, extinction — stressed on the right syllable.

band9.part1: Answer in two to four sentences: a direct answer, then a reason or tiny example. For "Did you have any pets growing up?" a Band 9 answer is particular: "We had a street dog who adopted us, really — she chose our gate and refused to leave, and after a week my father stopped pretending he minded." One real detail and a touch of humour beat a general statement about liking animals every time.
part2: Opening — name the animal and give one striking visual detail immediately; "the octopus — it's basically a brain with eight arms" earns attention faster than a slow build-up.
First encounter — where you met it: a childhood zoo visit, a documentary, a river near your grandparents' village. Ground it in a time and place.
The remarkable thing — pick ONE behaviour and go deep: how it changes colour, remembers faces, crosses oceans. One astonishing detail explained well beats five listed.
Bring it to life — a specific moment you watched or read about ("there's a clip where it unscrews a jar from the inside") gives the story its centre.
Your feelings — the fourth bullet wants emotion, not facts: name what watching it does to you — awe, unease, envy of its freedom — and let one sentence show it.
Concluding reflection — answer the explain line explicitly: why this animal over all others, and the thought it leaves you with about intelligence, nature, or us.

part3.method: Answer → Explain → Example → Alternative View → Evaluation
part3.question: Zoos say they exist for conservation and education. Critics say they're prisons with gift shops. Who's closer to the truth?
framework: Answer: commit with nuance — the critics are closer to the truth for most zoos, but the best zoos genuinely complicate the picture.

Explain: the mechanism — a zoo's income depends on visitors, so the animals people pay to see get kept whether or not keeping them serves any conservation purpose; the incentive runs against the mission.

Example: one concrete illustration — breeding programmes have genuinely saved species with almost none left in the wild, yet the same institutions keep elephants in enclosures a fraction of their natural range because elephants sell tickets.
Alternative view: concede genuinely — a child who stands in front of a real tiger may fund conservation for the rest of their life; screens don't seem to produce that conversion at the same rate.

Evaluate: land the judgement — so the fair test is whether an animal is there for its species' benefit or for ours, and most zoo residents fail it; the answer isn't closing zoos overnight but shrinking them around the animals that genuinely need them.

mistakes.title: Choosing an animal you know nothing about
mistakes.detail: Candidates pick the lion or dolphin because it sounds impressive, then run dry after 'it is very strong'. A crow you've actually watched steal food from your balcony gives you two minutes of real material; a half-remembered lion gives you thirty seconds.

mistakes.title: Reciting facts without feeling
mistakes.detail: The fourth bullet — how you feel watching it — is the one candidates drop, and it's what turns a Wikipedia summary into a Part 2 answer. The examiner is scoring your language for emotion and reflection, not your zoology.

mistakes.title: One-line Part 1 answers
mistakes.detail: "Dog person or cat person?" answered with "Dogs" goes nowhere. Two to four sentences with a because — and one small real detail — is the natural length.

mistakes.title: A memorised 'pollution' speech in Part 3
mistakes.detail: The conservation questions tempt candidates into a prepared environment essay. These questions are about animals, responsibility and public attention — a generic speech about plastic and factories answers none of them.

mistakes.title: Ducking the zoo question
mistakes.detail: It's deliberately two-sided and either verdict scores well. What fails is reciting 'zoos have advantages and disadvantages' and stopping — commit, then concede the other side its single best point.

mistakes.title: Only personal examples in Part 3
mistakes.detail: Your dog belongs in Part 2 and maybe one sentence of Part 3. The questions ask about cities, funding and societies — 'most urban families', 'donors in wealthy countries' — with your own pets as brief illustration at most.

mistakes.title: Repeating 'animal' and 'amazing' throughout
mistakes.detail: Vary both. Creature, species, wildlife, predator carry 'animal'; for 'amazing', say what is actually remarkable — uncanny, resourceful, eerily intelligent — or show it with the detail itself.

mistakes.title: Sentimentality instead of argument
mistakes.detail: "I love animals so much, they are so cute" is Band 5 filler in Part 3. Questions about advertising and conservation funding want mechanisms and trade-offs, delivered warmly if you like — but delivered.

mistakes.title: Guessing at species vocabulary
mistakes.detail: Inventing or mangling names ('the big water lizard of Africa') mid-story stalls fluency. If the English name won't come, describe and move on: 'a kind of wild goat that lives on cliffs' keeps the story running and shows paraphrase skill.

mistakes.title: Rushing the final abstract question
mistakes.detail: The humans-versus-animals question is the hardest in the set and invites a panicked sprint. Take the offered second, open with a stance, and slow down — a measured, stressed delivery on an abstract answer is exactly what Band 9 pronunciation looks like.
